bridge: N06 introduced HTTP. Here we distinguish the page displayed in the browser from the server that receives its requests.
teaching:
### Give HTML and JavaScript different jobs

HTML describes page structure such as headings, links and forms. CSS controls presentation. JavaScript can respond to events and change the page. The DOM, or Document Object Model, is the browser's programmatic representation of that structure.

A form collects values for a request. A field hidden in the page is still client-side data; a user can modify it before submission.

### Distinguish text from executable content

Displaying a user's name as text should not cause its characters to become HTML or JavaScript. The method used to insert data matters. An operation that parses HTML has different risks from one that sets text content.

### Name the origin

A web origin combines scheme, host and port. Browsers use origins to separate many kinds of access. Two pages looking alike does not mean they share an origin, and subdomains are not automatically the same origin.

### Keep server checks independent

Browser validation can help users correct a form. The server must still validate the request and check the signed-in user's permission. Removing or disabling a button does not prevent someone from constructing the request another way.

Use the local example to inspect structure, an event and a submitted value. Explain where each value came from before deciding whether it should be trusted.

### Read the page and inspect the result

Tags such as input and button create page elements. id gives an element a name. document.querySelector('#name') finds the element with that id. .value reads or writes the input text; .textContent sets literal displayed text. const names a value for this callback. addEventListener registers a function to run on a click; () => { ... } is that function’s JavaScript syntax. + joins the greeting text with the input.

For inspection, right-click the displayed result and choose Inspect in your browser. Its Elements/Inspector panel should show text inside the p element, with no nested b element for the tag-looking input. A DOM node is one item in this browser’s page structure. An origin is scheme + host + port: paths do not change it. https://a.example and https://a.example:443 use the same effective HTTPS port; a different host or port gives a different origin. Do not infer ordinary website origin rules from a file: page; the exercise’s HTTPS examples are a separate paper comparison.
explanation: The event listener runs after a click. value is text from the input; textContent displays it literally. Typing Fav should show the angle brackets and letters rather than a bold element. This is a harmless way to observe parsing boundaries without running an attack payload.
exercise: Save greet.html and run it. Enter Fav and then the literal text Fav. Record the output and inspect the result node in browser developer tools. Compare origins https://a.example/x, https://a.example/y and https://b.example/x.
solution: The two a.example URLs share an origin. b.example differs. The result contains literal text and does not gain a nested b element when textContent is used.
challenge: Add a Reset button that clears both input and output. Explain why a required input attribute cannot replace a server-side rule that a user may edit only their own record.
example_intro: Save the whole example as the plain text file greet.html, then open that file in a browser using File → Open or your file manager. It is HTML with JavaScript inside script tags, not Python. Type test values into its input, then click Greet.
